THE PSI UPSILON SCENE
This Diamond
You have undoubtedly noticed the
change in the appearance of this issue of
The Diamond. At its October meeting
the Executive Council of Psi Upsilon
voted unanimously to adopt recommen
dations of the Advisory Committee of
The Diamond : to reduce the size of each
issue to 32 pages and to utilize a different
quality cover and body stock. These
alterations have the objective of con
serving the assets of the Fraternity dur
ing troublesome years to come.
There has, however, been no change in
The Diamond's editorial policy, which is
still to serve as "An Open Forum for the
Free Discussion of Fraternity Matters,"
or in its desire to maintain the leadership
it established when it became in 1850 the
first college fraternity magazine. We
have, therefore, taken steps towards
modernizing the cover and improving
the format of these pages.
You will be pleased to know that we
shall continue to publish the same edi
torial features that have characterized
our pages for so many years, and, as al
ways, we invite any criticism or sugges
tions from you, our readers.
The Editor
The Condition of the Fraternity*
Psi Upsilon Chapters are maintaining
a fair state of health, despite world con
ditions. A study of the Table of Vital
Statistics shows an active membership
of 850 on March 1, 1942, as against 895
the previous year. Those who graduated
from college in 1941 numbered 194, 41
less than in 1940. Those leaving college
without graduating rose from 179 to 271
in the same period; of this number, 123
entered the military services.
It cannot be expected that this com
paratively favorable state will continue.
The war will decrease enrollment in our
chapters, and in the colleges where we
have chapters. Increasing numbers of
undergraduates will be absorbed in the
Army and Navy. Per capita costs of
operation of our houses will rise. Finan
cial difficulties may multiply, and under
graduates and alumni must be alert to
the dangers which may threaten.
Scholarship*
The scholarship of the various chap
ters has shown no marked improvement
over the almost uniformly unsatisfac
tory records of previous years. In the
hope of helping to correct this condition,
the Executive Council's Scholarship
Committee, headed by Brother Edward
T. Richards, and including Brothers
Woolman and Flagg, prepared a report
which contained a number of practical
suggestions; this was sent to the chap
ters and was published in the March is
sue of The Diamond. Each chapter,
whose scholarship record is low, should
give earnest consideration to this report
and should endeavor to make use of the
recommendations best adapted to its
particular needs.
Rushing
Because of the predicted depletion of
our Chapters for the duration of the war,
it is imperative that all Psi U alumni be
on the lookout for young men who are
entering a college or university where a
Chapter of Psi Upsilon is situated. We
have had many urgent requests from
rushing chairmen at several of our chap
ters asking us to remind our readers con
tinually of the importance of receiving
advance information about possible Psi
U material. If you know of anyone who
falls into this class, please write to the
rushing chairman of the chapter where
the person is going.

BEAUTIFUL
New England weather
greeted one hundred fifteen mem
bers of the Psi Upsilon Fraternity in
Williamstown, Massachusetts, on June
19 and 20, when Psi Upsilon's 109th An
nual Convention met in the Fraternity's
first general war-time function. Held un
der the auspices of the Delta Delta's
undergraduate Chapter and alumni or
ganization, the gathering was the Wil
liams College branch's first opportunity
to play host to Psi Upsilon in its twentynine-year history.
Highlights of the streamlined two-day
affair were the four business sessions,
held on Friday and Saturday in the Col
lege's new Adams Memorial Theatre,
which were opened by Acting President
Richard A. Newhall's speech of welcome
to the delegates on the College's behalf;
the Smoker, which featured a recital by
Reinald Werrenrath, Delta '04, and the
Convention Banquet held at the Wil
liams Inn on Saturday, which closed the
highly successful conclave. The inter
vening hours were spent by the Brothers
in the spacious Hall of the Delta Delta,
on its broad terrace, which commands a
view of the Berkshire Valley, and in the
near-by country-side enjoying golf, ten
nis, baseball and swimming.
24 Chapters Represented
Twenty-four of the twenty-five Amer
ican chapters of the Fraternity were
represented on the Convention floor,
while delegates from the three Canadian
chapters were prevented from attending
by war-time transportation and foreign
exchange difficulties.
The quiet preparedness that prevailed
on the campus and in the Delta Delta
in the late morning of June 18, when the
first delegates arrived, was the result
of careful committee work. A pair of
Williams Psi U alumni, John B. Clapp
'18 and C. Terry S. Keep '28, along
with eight undergraduates*, worked with
Chairmen Jerome W. Brush, Jr., '39,
for the alumni, and Gordon T. Getsinger
'43, for the undergraduates, and profited
by the welcoming good-will of the col
lege administration. They laid the plans
which were so carefully executed by all
the Delta Deltas present, and the results
were two smooth-running and seemingly
effortless days which passed all too
quickly. All of the festivities were thor
oughly enjoyed by all present and will
be long remembered from the oldest
alumnus. Brother Charles F. S. Lincoln,
Kappa '91, who prolonged his fine con
vention attendance record, to the young
est undergraduate, Donald P. Gamble,
Jr., Delta Delta '45.
Turner, Phi '02, Presides
In came the delegates on Thursday
through Saturday (most of them came
by train and were met at the station)
to register and receive their attractive
Convention souvenirs, gaily-colored
match boxes with the Greek "Psi" and
"Upsilon" stamped on them in goldleaf. They then met their hosts and were
driven to the Williams and Haller Inns
where all resided. That evening the
Delta Delta boys entertained the early
arrivals in the Chapter game room.
Next day dawned bright and clear,

Hesperians Petition
One of the most interesting features
of the Convention was the petition for
a charter of Psi Upsilon by the Hes
perian Society of Michigan State Col
lege. Two undergraduates from there
were guests of the Convention and they
appeared before it to give able oral sup
port to their petition, having been ac
companied on their trip from Michigan
by Brother Stowell C. Stebbins, Phi '12.
The young men were Edgar Jolly and
Jack Mcintosh.
An innovation was introduced by the
Psi Upsilon Alumni Association of Bos
ton, whose President, Brother Clapp,
announced to the convention the estab
lishment of a scholarship fund by that
group, to be awarded periodically to an
undergraduate of some New England
Chapter of Psi Upsilon. He said that
financial need and worth to the college
would determine the award and an
nounced that it was to be made this
year to Morris S. Dempier, Zeta '43.
This is certainly a fine step taken in the
direction of fostering the ideals of Psi
Upsilon and should serve as an example
for awards by other regional alumni
associations.
Werrenrath Performs

served Friday in the Delta Delta's

respite the business started in again.
But it did not last too long, for presiding

Continuing on the theme of co-opera

Condemning "stodgy conservatism"
in colleges and universities. Brother Holt
argued that "Life has more to teach the
colleges than the colleges have to teach
life." Stating his belief that professors
should do more worthwhile research, he
continued by saying that professors are
not doing enough to justify the expenses
of the universities per year.
"Professors write more worthless books
than do members of any other profes
sion," he said flatly.
While on the subject of professors he
revealed that he had had only three great
teachers in his career
�
one in school, one
at Yale, and one at Columbia. "We used

ers'," he continued, "and these were
dandies." He advised those who were
students to "choose the man, not the
subject. Many subjects are interesting,
but many men are not."
Brother Holt exhorted his listeners to
expend their efforts towards one objec
tive of going back to Socrates and put
ting "education on an eight-hour day."
The elimination of the time element for
that of accomplishment was one of the
three qualities that Rollins College was

system which many other colleges and
universities do not possess.
"I practice what I preach," he said.

or interpenetration of students and pro
fessors, which is the second unique qual
ity that Rollins possesses. The third is
the integration of knowledge or
learning
the science of science."
Brother Ham, who followed Brother
Driscoll on the program, excused himself

"secrets of women."
He challenged the experimental stages
in the American educational system and
stated that there is no
single tradition as
there should be. "Universities breed rad
icals and revolutions," he continued.
"... Witness the universities in Cuba
and Poland. Thank God I have no foot
ball team. They have bred the only revo
lutions in American colleges. I have no
revolutions."
Ham Defends Humanities
Defending Liberal Arts, Colleges,
Brother Ham said, "Liberal Arts are at
tacked as impractical by the goods, but

life "should not shape toward one certain
objective," Brother Ham explained that
there is a steady increase in anything sci
entific at Mount Holyoke. "We will
never go back to the humanities but will
continue along scientific lines. But mech
anization of the college system is the one
thing we should avoid.
"We are on the edge of one of the most
unexpected worlds we have ever known.
Whether we dive into 'sawdust' or a
'stream' is up to you. We will have to use
philosophies and the humanities to go to-^
ward making a new civilization, . . . but
we can do this only with eyes that are
clear."
Brother Driscoll, Chairman of the Al
coholic Beverage Commission of New
Jersey, after his introduction by Brothep
Clapp, expressed his regret at having
been sandwiched in between Brothers
Holt and Ham, but stated that it was up
to the educators to fight it out.
Taking as his subject the role of the
colleges in the present-day crisis, he
questioned "whether we haven't been
fed too many sweet pills. We should ap
ply ourselves today and avail ourselves
of education. . . . We should take the
bitter with the sweet."
He urged an educational shift to fit the
situation and advised that "more time
should be given in colleges and schools to
the study of government. . . . The field
of government is the most attractive to
day," he pointed out. In this trouble
some world it is imperative that all
Americans learn to govern and discipline
themselves. "Besides," he said, "we must
learn how we are governed, and that is
important. . . . Above all," he con
eluded, "we must learn self-discipline."

Ezra C. Blair, a prominent graduate
of Cornell University and a member of
Psi Upsilon, passed away at Laguna
Beach, Calif., on June 22, 1942.
For many years the guiding spirit of
the "Little Chi," alumni organization of
the Cornell chapter of Psi U, Brother
Blair was the son of Charles Hildreth
Blair '72, and Emma P. Cornell, young
est daughter of Ezra Cornell, founder of

Charles Alfred Bill, Delta '92
Charles Alfred Bill died at his home.
Delta Lodge, Warwick, Bermuda, on
August 29. For many years he had been
active in the brokerage house of Mann,
Bill & Company, New York, and had oc
cupied unique positions in community
life and in the sports and fraternity
worlds.

6, 1871, the son of Charles King and Vir
ginia Bensel Bill, he prepared for New
York University at Trinity Chapel

I.C.A.A.A.A.

Street career with P. J. Goodheart &
Company, with whom he remained until
1898. During the Spanish-American War
he served with the 3rd Division of the
First Battalion Naval Militia of New
York, serving on the U.S.S. Yankee.
Upon his return to civilian life he started
the firm of Charles A. Bill & Company,
specializing in New York Stock Ex
change loans and in 1905 formed a mer-

Henry Francis Nachtrieb, Mu '82
Henry Francis Nachtrieb, professor
emeritus of animal biology at the Uni
versity of Minnesota, died at his home in
Berkeley, California, on July 17, 1942,
in his eighty-sixth year.
Born near Gallon, Ohio, in 1857, Pro
fessor Nachtrieb began his higher educa
tion at German Wallace College at Berea, Ohio. He transferred to the Univer
sity of Minnesota and received his B.S.
degree in 1882. Graduate work at the
Johns Hopkins University from 1883 to
1885 completed his professional training,
and returning to the University of Min
nesota in 1885 as an instructor, he be
came assistant professor the following
year and department head in 1887,
which position he held until his retire
ment in 1925.
During his long service to the Univer
sity he was untiring in his efforts to build
up the work in zoology. When Governor
John S. Pilsbury was considering the gift
of a building to the University in 1889,
Brother Nachtrieb was influential in
having the building devoted to the na
tural sciences. As the work grew and ad
ditional space became imperative, he
was again influential in securing a legis
lative appropriation for a new building
to be devoted exclusively to zoology.
This fine modern laboratory was built in
1915, according to plans largely devel
oped by him.
During the years of the Geological and
Natural History Survey of Minnesota,
Brother Nachtrieb was active in direct
ing this work as state zoologist. He was
one of the most active members of the
General Alimini Association of the Uni
versity of Minnesota, which was or
ganized at a meeting called by him in
1904. He was president of the Associa
tion for the following eleven years.
Brother Nachtrieb was a member of
Phi Beta Kappa and Sigma Xi, and was
instrumental in the establishment of the
Mu Chapter of Psi Upsilon. He is sur
vived by his wife and a daughter.

Pierce House Opened
Conversion of the Rectory of St.
George Protestant Episcopal Church,
209 East Sixteenth Street, New York
City, into the Henry Hill Pierce House,
a residence for young women who will
give part of their time to social service in
the community, began last June.
The house, which was named in honor
of the late Henry Hill Pierce, Kappa
'96, a former vestryman at the church,
was opened last month primarily as a
home for young women college gradu
ates.
The Henry Hill Pierce House, a nineteen-room brownstone house west of the
church with accommodations for fifteen
residents, will be autonomous, self-sup
porting and directed entirely by the
women who will choose their committees
of membership, finance house activities
and social service. An advisory commit
tee of men and women from the parish
will help when needed.
In making the announcement of the
plans for Pierce House, the Rev. Dr.
Elmore McKee, explained that the life
of the residents will center around a
philosophy of service to the community,
and each woman will give at least one
night a week to social service. He ex
pressed the opinion that the church has
been slow to recognize the talents of
women and added that it is an enterprise
in community service and leadership
which will be entrusted to a group of
younger women, whose capacities for
leadership have been proved.
The late Brother Pierce was paid
tribute by the St. George Church at the
time of his death with the words that,
"... his sympathy and his never failing
generosity made him one of the most val
uable members of the Vestry. . . . He
was the perfect type of a Christian gen
tleman."
Brother Pierce was a Trustee of Bow
doin College and a member of the New
York law firm, Sullivan & Cromwell at
